subject: physics
question_text: Define one calorie. Define the mechanical equivalent of heat.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 12 Very Short Answer Question 7 (printed p.124). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The two-way mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: one calorie raises the temperature of one gram of water from 14.5 °C to 15.5 °C at one atmosphere; W = JQ defines the mechanical equivalent of heat J, with J ≈ 4.186 J cal⁻¹ (about 4.2), the conversion factor between calories and joules.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: One calorie
lines: One calorie is the heat needed to
raise the temperature of one gram
at a pressure of one atmosphere.
steps.margin_note: First mark. State the definition — one gram of water from 14.5 °C to 15.5 °C; the one-atmosphere condition secures it.
steps.why: The range 14.5 °C to 15.5 °C is fixed because the specific heat of water changes slightly with temperature, so the calorie needs one fixed interval to have a single value.
common_mistakes: Giving a rounded range such as 14 °C to 15 °C instead of the exact 14.5 °C to 15.5 °C.
Leaving out the pressure condition of one atmosphere — add it to secure the answer.

recall.must_convey: That one calorie is the heat needed to raise the temperature of one gram of water from 14.5 degrees Celsius to 15.5 degrees Celsius at one atmosphere pressure.
accept: one gram of water by one degree
heard_as: fourteen point five to fifteen point five

steps.memory_tip: One gram, one degree, from 14.5 to 15.5 °C, at one atmosphere.

steps.label: Mechanical equivalent
lines: The mechanical equivalent of heat J
is the ratio of mechanical work
done to the heat it produces:
steps.margin_note: Second mark. W = JQ, then J ≈ 4.186 J cal⁻¹, about 4.2.
steps.why: J is the factor that converts a quantity of heat, measured in calories, into the same quantity measured as mechanical work in joules — a conversion factor, not a new form of energy.
common_mistakes: Writing Q = JW with J and Q swapped — work equals J times the heat, W = JQ.
Giving J without its value, about 4.2 joules per calorie.

recall.must_convey: That the mechanical equivalent of heat J is the ratio of work done to heat produced, W equals J times Q, and J is about 4.2 joules per calorie.
accept: four point two joules per calorie
reject: one gram of water by one degree

steps.memory_tip: J converts calories to joules — about 4.2 joules for every calorie.

insider_note: The calorie's range, 14.5 °C to 15.5 °C, and J's value, about 4.2 J cal⁻¹, are the two numbers checked most often.
